full_judgment:
69. There is a presumption against, the taking away of a vested right by repeal or amendment of the law. Of course, this presumption is rebuttable if the enquiry reveals "express enactment or necessary intendment contrary to the presumption". Vested right are preserved by legal presumption, unless those are destroyed by an enactment. In Colonial Sugar Refining Co. Ltd. Vs. Irving case the rule of law has been clearly enunciated the "while provisions of a statute dealing merely with matters of procedure may properly, unless that construction be textually inadmissible have retrospective effect attributed Jo them provisions which touch a right in existence as the passing of the statute are not to be applied retrospectively in the absence of express enactment or necessary intendment". It has been held therein that in principle there is no difference between abolishing an appeal altogether: and transferring an appeal to a new forum because, in either case there is an interference with existing rights contrary to the well-known general principle that statutes are not to be held Jo act retrospectively unless a clear intention to that effect is manifested. In the present case it is not a simple case of change of forum of appeal only. It has been pointed out above the extent of major changes causing material disadvantages involved in taking an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal in place of the High Court Division which amounts Jo denial of justice. 

 70. There is a presumption that the legislature intended its enactments to have prospective operation. This is because of the basic presumption that the legislature does not intent to enact legislation which operates oppressively and retrospective laws will generally have sub operation. For giving retrospective construction to a statute, its language must imperatively and clearly require so. In this context reference may be made to Crawford on Statutory Construction. According to Crawford, in the absence of any indication in the statute that the legislature intended it to operate retrospectively, it must not, be given retrospective effect. If perchance any reasonable doubt exists, it should be resolved in favor of prospective operation. In other words, before a law will be construed as retrospective, its language must imperatively and clearly require such a construction. Moreover, in this connection, as a general rule, a statute expressed in general terms will be given prospective effect, and considered applicable to conditions coming into existence subsequent to its enactment, even though they were not actually known at the time of enactment. But where an intention properly appears that the statute was intended to operate retrospectively, such operation must be confined as closely as possible. 

 71. If the language of sub-section (1) and (2) of section 30 is carefully examined it will appear that the legislature did not intend even that new section 30 Jo come into effect immediately on the enactment, that is, with effect from July 29, 1974. In sub-sect ion (1) it has been provided that an appeal from the judgment of or sentence passed by a Special Tribunal may be preferred to the Appellate Tribunal, constituted under subsection (2). Sub-section (2) provides that the Government shall, for the purpose of this Act, constitute an Appellate Tribunal consisting of one member to be appointed by the Government. Thus it appears that so long the Appellate Tribunal was not constituted in the manner as provided in sub-section (2), there was no scope for subsection (1) of section 30 coming into effect. We have been informed that the Appellate Tribunal, as a matter of fact, was constituted on November 2, 1974, that is, after more than three months. If we accept the view adverted by the learned Attorney-General, the result would be that against the judgments delivered or sentences passed during the period between July 29 and November 2, 1974. There would be no appeal, as there was no forum of appeal. Confronted with this situation the learned Attorney-General also felt it difficult to explain this anomalous position. Basic presumption is that the legislature does not intend to enact a legislation which operates oppressively and unjustly. After examining the language of section 30 from various aspects we have no doubt that section 30 is prospective in operation" and it does not affect the rights that accrued, particularly the right of appeal to the High Court Division of The Supreme Court accrued in the pending proceedings. In such matters forum of appeal will still continue there as provided in the repealed section 30. Therefore, our answer to the first question is that appeals from the judgments and sentences passed by the Special Tribunals in the proceedings pending at the re-enactment of section 30, lie to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court and not to the Appellate Tribunal. Since forum of appeals from judgments and sentences passed by the Special Tribunals in the proceedings pending prior to the amendment is not the Appellate Tribunal, the question of the High Court Division ceasing to have the jurisdiction to entertain appeals, if the some were not pending on the date of amendment, does not arise. In the result, we hold that the appeal is maintainable.
